title: No design, incomplete load path, ongoing investigation: temporary works control still matters
excerpt: June 2026 HSE fines followed a City of London temporary platform collapse with no design or safe-load calculation. CROSS-UK Report 1539 (May 2026) records propping issued without verifying the existing structure could carry redistributed loads. An HSE investigation continues after the 21 October 2026 Banbury scaffolding and building partial collapse. Contractors must keep temporary structures inside the BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM process: design brief, verified load path, register, permit and competent supervision.
linkedinReady:
Temporary wooden platforms that collect concrete debris still need a design and a safe working load.

In June 2026 the Health and Safety Executive reported that two companies were fined after a temporary platform collapsed during floor cutting in the City of London, fracturing a worker’s neck and back. The investigation found no design for the platforms and no calculation of safe loading. The person completing the inspection form was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to clear debris were not enough without a defined load limit and monitoring.

CROSS-UK Report 1539 (published May 2026) shows a parallel gap in propping. Heavy-duty props were issued for column replacement, but the designer had not checked whether the existing beams and slab could transfer the redistributed loads. Once opened up, the beams and slab were shown to be inadequate in bending and shear. Without further temporary works the building could have partially collapsed.

An ongoing HSE investigation follows the partial collapse of scaffolding and an apartment block under construction in Banbury on 21 October 2026. Two of nine workers were hospitalised. Details of cause remain under enquiry; the practical reminder is that scaffolding and temporary stability systems must stay within the project temporary works procedure.

BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM 2015 require a controlled process: design brief, competent design and check, live register, permit to load, and competent supervision. Temporary structures are not “just timber” or “just props.” They carry foreseeable loads and must have a verified load path from the point of application to a suitable foundation or support.

Identify the temporary condition. Design or confirm a standard solution within its limits. Check it. Permit it. Inspect it. Strike it under control.

Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 15 June 2026 HSE published the outcome of prosecutions against Roots Contractors Limited and Diacutt Limited following a February 2024 incident at Paxton House, City of London. Temporary wooden platforms built to collect concrete cores and debris collapsed onto a drilling operative working below, causing fractures to the neck and back and a brain bleed. HSE found no design for the platforms and no calculation of a safe level of loading. An inspection form was completed by a person who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Verbal instructions to clear platforms existed, but no safe load was known and clearing was not monitored. Planning, supervision and coordination of the drilling work were also deficient.

CROSS-UK Report 1539, published 14 May 2026, describes temporary works for replacement of a defective reinforced concrete column in a multi-storey block of flats. Heavy-duty props had already been installed and a drawing issued. The props themselves were capable of the required forces, but no evidence was found that the prop designer had checked the existing structure. Opening-up showed that the existing beams and slab were not strong enough to transfer the redistributed loads and would fail in bending and shear. The Reporter designed additional temporary works and a method statement. Without those measures a significant part of the building could have collapsed. The Expert Panel noted the need for a verified load path from the point of application through to a suitable support, and for the temporary works procedure (including TWC and checking) to be applied.

On 21 October 2026 scaffolding and an apartment block under construction partially collapsed in Cherwell Street, Banbury. Nine workers were on site; two were taken to hospital. HSE is investigating. Oxfordshire County Council partially reopened the road on 30 October after safety advice, with further temporary closures expected for crane operations to make the site safe. No confirmed cause has been published; the reminder for contractors is that scaffolding and temporary stability systems remain subject to the project temporary works procedure while the investigation continues.

ul: Treat any temporary platform, crash deck, propping system or scaffold as a temporary works item requiring entry on the live Temporary Works Register.
Issue a design brief that defines foreseeable loads, including debris accumulation, and confirm either a project-specific design or a standard solution used strictly within its stated limits.
When propping or supporting an existing structure, require verification of the full load path, including capacity of beams, slabs, walls and foundations that will receive redistributed loads.
Ensure the person completing inspections or issuing permits is a competent Temporary Works Coordinator or Supervisor under the project procedure.
Do not load, alter or strike temporary works until a formal permit has been issued after the required checks.
Maintain documented supervision and clear communication so that workers are not placed under unauthorised or overloaded temporary structures.
Close the register entry only after verification, acceptance and controlled striking under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Subject to project-specific verification and acceptance under the project temporary works procedure. Exact clause references in BS 5975-1:2024 and other standards to be confirmed against the project’s licensed copy. AI-generated or third-party summaries require competent review before use on site. Cause of the Banbury incident remains under HSE investigation; no findings are stated here.
